Spotlight

Announcing Institutional Fellowships!

By Shewanee Howard-Baptiste, Provost

We are delighted to announce the appointment of our inaugural Institutional Fellows, whose work will advance innovation, collaboration, and institutional effectiveness across the college.

Dr. Mario Nakazawa has been selected as the Institutional Fellow for Amplifying Human Intelligence in the World of AI, where he will explore meaningful ways to leverage artificial intelligence to enhance teaching, learning, scholarship, and human potential.

Dr. Angie Cox and Dr. Neil Mecham have been appointed as Institutional Fellows for Developing a Framework for Faculty Workload: Credit Hours and Teaching Load. Working collaboratively, they will examine best practices and develop recommendations to support a transparent, equitable, and sustainable approach to faculty workload.

Dan Adams has been selected as the Institutional Fellow for Staff Compensation Study and Staff Workload (Berea Balance). He will work in partnership with multiple campus partners to strategize ways to enhance staff needs and support.

Please join us in congratulating Mario, Angie, Neil, and Dan on their selection as our first Institutional Fellows. We look forward to the insight, leadership, and impact they will bring to these important initiatives.

Feature

VitalSource Vitals: Inclusive Access, What Is It?

By Shannon Purtee

Many of you have either utilized VitalSource's Inclusive Access Program or have shown an interest in IA. Inclusive Access means your students' digital course materials are waiting for them in the bookstore or LMS on day one. Enrollment in the program means the students don't need to purchase that book within the bookstore; therefore, it does not take away from the $500 credit line available for students to charge their student account. Most books are available for enrollment in IA, and it is done at your discretion on a book-by-book basis. The cost is added automatically to the student's bookstore account unless they opt out.

That's the detail faculty get asked about most: every student should log into the bookstore site early in the term, even if they don't plan to purchase anything, since that's the only place to see their Inclusive Access materials and opt out if they'd rather go another route. Students have a very short window to opt out before they are charged, and that charge is not reversible. However, if they opt out accidentally, we do have the ability to put them back in IA. A quick mention in your syllabus and first-week announcements can save students a lot of confusion and unexpected charges later. The link below is an informational sheet you can provide to your students as well.

Bookstore Ordering Instructions for Students

Have a VitalSource Vital topic you feel should be in future editions? Contact Shannon Purtee to share, and for any bookstore questions or concerns: purtees@berea.edu.

Build It Once: A Reusable AI Check for Accessible Documents

By Rob Smith, Executive Director of Institutional Effectiveness and Accreditation

By now, all of us know the importance of our documents being accessible. However, very few of us have time to check every syllabus, handout, form, and PowerPoint slide by hand. But this is one practical way of using AI to help improve those work products while saving you time. Most AI tools have a feature that allows you to build a set of automatic and reusable instructions that will carry out a complex series of tasks without you having to spell those out each time. They're called skills, and they're nothing more than a simple text file that you save to wherever your AI tool stores these specialized pre-built instruction sets. The nice part is that your AI tool knows exactly when to invoke that particular skill because you specify, as part of the skill, when it should be invoked.

I use one that I built for exactly this purpose. First, my AI tool audits any document against WCAG 2.2 AA, the current web accessibility guidelines. Based on that audit, it tells me what part(s) fail(s), where, and why. Then, after I approve, it revises that document according to the WCAG 2.2 AA standard. It sorts corrections into three groups: ones it can make safely (e.g., a missing document title), those it drafts for me but needs me to approve (e.g., alt text, link wording), and ones it leaves entirely to me (e.g., whether an image is decorative, or anything that changes meaning).

If I've piqued your interest, I've posted a version of that skill as a file anyone can download. Download the accessibility skill file here.

If you use BoodleBox (our approved campus-wide tool), you simply upload it to the Skills page found under the "Banks" icon in the left nav menu. Once it's been loaded, you can invoke that skill in any future chat simply by typing a forward slash (/) followed by "accessibility-check". If Claude or ChatGPT is your preferred AI tool, the process is much the same, except you can simply drag and drop the file in a chat window and type "Install the attached skill". I also recommend checking out these guides from Claude ai and ChatGPT on how to create and use skills. As always, though, you should still verify the output using your own knowledge about accessibility standards.

If you're interested in other ways that you can use AI to improve accessibility for you, your colleagues, or your students, don't forget to check out this month's AI Ready series sponsored by the Council of Independent Colleges (CIC). October's focus is all about using AI to enhance or improve the accessibility of your workflow. You can register at the following link: October Webinars on AI as an Accessibility Tool.

Big Savings: Wrapping Up Year 3 of the Free Textbook Program

By Jade Stiles

The Free Textbook Program, a collaboration between Hutchins Library and the Office of Sustainability, wrapped up its third fall distribution with record-breaking impact. This semester, students picked up nearly 400 books out of the available titles, saving patrons $15,982 on course materials, nearly doubling the $8,940 saved in fall 2024.

The program begins each spring when the Office of Sustainability collects donated textbooks through Green Move Out. Over the summer, Hutchins Library organizes the collection for fall distribution. This year, we introduced an online store via CampusGroups, allowing students to browse inventory and place holds ahead of time while also providing better tracking of the supplied materials.

Special thanks go to the Reference student assistants for managing online holds, Campus Life for technical guidance with CampusGroups, and the Office of Sustainability for powering collections. Remaining books will be stored to support future semesters as the program continues reducing waste and course costs.

We look forward to saving the campus community more money in the spring!

Announcement

AI Ready Webinars: Cheating, Authorship, and Academic Trust

November's topic in the AI Ready webinar series is Cheating, Authorship, and Academic Trust, a three-part series held on three Thursdays in November, all from 2:00 to 3:00 PM Eastern: Nov. 5, 12, and 19. Each one-hour session looks at real-world use cases, ethical questions, and institutional strategies around AI and academic integrity: what counts as cheating, how authorship should be attributed, and how we sustain trust among students, instructors, and institutions.

There is no cost to participate, and everyone is welcome. Once you register, you'll receive a Zoom link with all the information you need. Register here: November Webinars on Cheating, Authorship, and Academic Trust.

Feature

On My Radar: Ideas, Initiatives & Projects in Motion

By Mary Robert Garrett, Associate Provost and Dean of Faculty

You'll usually hear about my work through other channels, so here's a glimpse at a few projects I've got going on:

  • I'm identifying funding agencies that support faculty and staff development at small liberal arts colleges. My hope is to expand opportunities at Berea that could potentially include travel experiences. Opportunities like these strengthen professional work and build community across campus. I'll keep you posted!
  • With this fall's enrollment boom, I was curious about our average class sizes and how many students faculty see each week. Here's what I found:
    • Faculty teaching a full three-course load this term see an average of 45 students per week (SD = 14). The range runs from 21 to 74 students.
    • To include everyone, I also looked at students per teaching-load credit. The average is 15 students (SD = 4.4), ranging from 7 to 33. (This loosely translates to average class size.)
    • Faculty are using 23 course releases and 4.5 credit overloads this term.
  • I'm developing strategies to navigate challenging conversations with empathy, perspective, and resilience. I will continue to create an environment where colleagues feel heard and supported, particularly during times of uncertainty, while maintaining healthy boundaries that allow me to remain focused on our shared goals.
Feature

What We're Reading

Tiffany Lindsey

Holding Space: A Storytelling Approach to Trampling Diversity and Inclusion by Aminata Cairo

It presents a unique framework for equity and inclusion that moves beyond traditional corporate or institutional diversity models.

Mary Robert Garrett

The Bell Jar by Sylvia Plath

A friend who is working through a list of great American authors this academic year recommended this novel to me. I knew Plath as an influential poet but had never read her prose. [Spoiler alert] The novel follows a young woman's slow descent into depression and a suicide attempt. Since Plath herself died by suicide at just 30, shortly after the book was published, I was curious how she would portray that path through a character. The story is heavy and emotionally challenging to read (depending on your level of empathy), but the imagery is striking and clearly the work of a gifted poet.

Rob Smith

Co-Intelligence: Living and Working with AI by Ethan Mollick

This is a practical guide to working with generative AI as a capable but unpredictable collaborator, where you learn its strengths and limits by using it and staying critically involved. I'm re-reading this in anticipation of his follow-up book, Co-Existence: The Next Phase of AI, due to be released soon!

Joe Murphy

The Sacred Art of Teaching: The Delpit/Emdin Conversations by Lisa Delpit & Christopher Emdin

This is a transcribed series of informal conversations between two award-winning educators and authors, and I'm thoroughly enjoying their interaction. It's a much different way of seeing minds and personalities at work than you get in most academic books about teaching and learning. I'm excited by the way they talk about critical and liberatory pedagogies, and at the same time I'm thinking through the way the experience of two K-12 educators, rooted in the Black Teaching Tradition, does and doesn't transfer to our practices in higher ed.

Announcement

Conversations and Connections with Academic Affairs

Sponsored by the Office for Community & Commitments and the Loyal Jones Appalachian Center

Wednesday, November 4th · 12:00 to 1:15 PM · Legacy Hall Training Room · Lunch provided

Led by Dr. Christopher Miller, College Curator

College Curator Christopher Miller will lead an exploration of how the material aspects of places (objects, landscapes, and human bodies) are involved in the emergence of community. The program will feature artifacts from the Appalachian Artifact Teaching Collection and draw from Miller's research with Practice Theory. It will involve a mixture of lecture, storytelling, artifact handling, and conversation. Miller believes that learning to work and study in a world of AI requires people to become more deliberate and thoughtful at engaging the tangible and material world, not because it is better than AI but because we tend to not notice it, like a fish and the water in which it swims.
